sources.title: Tips, Tricks, and Books for Helping Kids Understand Calendars
sources.publisher: Brightly (Penguin Random House), written by a kindergarten and preschool teacher
sources.quote: explanations like “on Wednesday,” “in a week,” or “in the fall” feel arbitrary when you’re little. ... Kids are more likely to internalize calendar concepts and patterns when they can put them in the context of their own lives. ... Ask them to point to “yesterday, today, and tomorrow,” find specific day numbers, or count the days or weeks until a significant event. ... Of course, there are lots of great books that help kids commit the days of the week and months of the year to memory, too.
sources.supports: A week or a month is an abstract unit for a young child; a calendar used to count the days until an event, and time tied to things from the child's own life, make it concrete. A US early educator's parenting article, applied to Israeli families as general advice.

sources.title: Create a Kid's Calendar in Two Ways
sources.quote: Waiting for big events like birthdays, holidays, or the start of school are great opportunities to for your child to learn to keep track of days and months. ... Invite your child to decorate day squares on a store-bought or recycled calendar to reflect some of the activities that they do on certain days. ... Encourage your child to number the days of the month and decorate the calendar with pictures, stickers, or other craft supplies.
sources.supports: Waiting for a birthday is an occasion to learn to track days; the child decorates and numbers the squares of a calendar with pictures and stickers.

sources.title: How to help your preschooler manage overexcitement
sources.quote: Plan on giving a five-minute notice when you see they start to get louder and too excited. ... It may help your preschooler if you have an agreed-upon signal to give them when they seem to be getting too excited. ... Making your child more aware of how they act and feel when they’re getting overexcited can eventually help your child stay calmer.
sources.supports: A five-minute notice, an agreed signal and naming what you see when a preschooler gets overexcited. The page is about overexcitement in general; applied to the days before a birthday. No promise of a result.

sources.title: Tips, Tricks, and Books for Helping Kids Understand Calendars
sources.publisher: Brightly (Penguin Random House), written by a kindergarten and preschool teacher
sources.quote: explanations like “on Wednesday,” “in a week,” or “in the fall” feel arbitrary when you’re little. ... Kids are more likely to internalize calendar concepts and patterns when they can put them in the context of their own lives. ... Ask them to point to “yesterday, today, and tomorrow,” find specific day numbers, or count the days or weeks until a significant event. ... Of course, there are lots of great books that help kids commit the days of the week and months of the year to memory, too.
sources.supports: A week or a month is an abstract unit for a young child; a calendar used to count the days until an event, and time tied to things from the child's own life, make it concrete. A US early educator's parenting article, applied to Israeli families as general advice.

sources.title: Create a Kid's Calendar in Two Ways
sources.quote: Waiting for big events like birthdays, holidays, or the start of school are great opportunities to for your child to learn to keep track of days and months. ... Invite your child to decorate day squares on a store-bought or recycled calendar to reflect some of the activities that they do on certain days. ... Encourage your child to number the days of the month and decorate the calendar with pictures, stickers, or other craft supplies.
sources.supports: Waiting for a birthday is an occasion to learn to track days; the child decorates and numbers the squares of a calendar with pictures and stickers.

sources.title: How to help your preschooler manage overexcitement
sources.quote: Plan on giving a five-minute notice when you see they start to get louder and too excited. ... It may help your preschooler if you have an agreed-upon signal to give them when they seem to be getting too excited. ... Making your child more aware of how they act and feel when they’re getting overexcited can eventually help your child stay calmer.
sources.supports: A five-minute notice, an agreed signal and naming what you see when a preschooler gets overexcited. The page is about overexcitement in general; applied to the days before a birthday. No promise of a result.

sources.title: Tips, Tricks, and Books for Helping Kids Understand Calendars
sources.publisher: Brightly (Penguin Random House), written by a kindergarten and preschool teacher
sources.quote: explanations like “on Wednesday,” “in a week,” or “in the fall” feel arbitrary when you’re little. ... Kids are more likely to internalize calendar concepts and patterns when they can put them in the context of their own lives. ... Ask them to point to “yesterday, today, and tomorrow,” find specific day numbers, or count the days or weeks until a significant event. ... Of course, there are lots of great books that help kids commit the days of the week and months of the year to memory, too.
sources.supports: A week or a month is an abstract unit for a young child; a calendar used to count the days until an event, and time tied to things from the child's own life, make it concrete. A US early educator's parenting article, applied to Israeli families as general advice.

sources.title: Create a Kid's Calendar in Two Ways
sources.quote: Waiting for big events like birthdays, holidays, or the start of school are great opportunities to for your child to learn to keep track of days and months. ... Invite your child to decorate day squares on a store-bought or recycled calendar to reflect some of the activities that they do on certain days. ... Encourage your child to number the days of the month and decorate the calendar with pictures, stickers, or other craft supplies.
sources.supports: Waiting for a birthday is an occasion to learn to track days; the child decorates and numbers the squares of a calendar with pictures and stickers.

sources.title: How to help your preschooler manage overexcitement
sources.quote: Plan on giving a five-minute notice when you see they start to get louder and too excited. ... It may help your preschooler if you have an agreed-upon signal to give them when they seem to be getting too excited. ... Making your child more aware of how they act and feel when they’re getting overexcited can eventually help your child stay calmer.
sources.supports: A five-minute notice, an agreed signal and naming what you see when a preschooler gets overexcited. The page is about overexcitement in general; applied to the days before a birthday. No promise of a result.

sources.quote: an unwillingness to share is perfectly normal at this age! ... It is okay to let children have a “long turn” ... Help the other child wait by offering a different activity. ... The great thing about the timer is that it’s not the adult telling the children when to share, it’s the “bell.” ... It’s OK to be upset when you have to wait. Waiting is hard!
sources.supports: Not sharing is normal for toddlers and preschoolers; a long turn, a different activity for the waiting child, a timer as the rule-keeper and naming that waiting is hard.

sources.title: Helping Kids Learn to Take Turns and Practice Waiting
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents (Samantha Gratton), 4 Aug 2023
sources.quote: Practice beforehand, showing your child how to use their words when asking for a turn. ... If your child thinks someone’s turn is taking too long, help them practice asking, “Can you take a shorter turn, please?” ... In “Daniel Tiger’s Neighborhood,” Daniel and his friends have many opportunities to take turns at school and while playing at the pool.
sources.supports: Practising in advance how to ask for a turn with words, including asking for a shorter turn; a children's story (Daniel Tiger's Neighborhood) used to model taking turns. A US public media parenting article.

sources.title: Getting Preschoolers to Share…How Do You Do It?
sources.publisher: Pathways.org (pediatric therapists' nonprofit, last updated 18 Jul 2025)
sources.quote: If your child has a toy that is their absolute favorite that they do not want to share, put it away before the play date! ... Something visual, like a timer, will let children know exactly when it’s time for them to give up a certain toy.
sources.supports: A favorite toy can be put away before a playdate; a visual timer shows when it is time to hand over a toy.

sources.title: Helping Young Children With Sharing
sources.quote: an unwillingness to share is perfectly normal at this age! ... It is okay to let children have a “long turn” ... Help the other child wait by offering a different activity. ... The great thing about the timer is that it’s not the adult telling the children when to share, it’s the “bell.” ... It’s OK to be upset when you have to wait. Waiting is hard!
sources.supports: Not sharing is normal for toddlers and preschoolers; a long turn, a different activity for the waiting child, a timer as the rule-keeper and naming that waiting is hard.

sources.title: Helping Kids Learn to Take Turns and Practice Waiting
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents (Samantha Gratton), 4 Aug 2023
sources.quote: Practice beforehand, showing your child how to use their words when asking for a turn. ... If your child thinks someone’s turn is taking too long, help them practice asking, “Can you take a shorter turn, please?” ... In “Daniel Tiger’s Neighborhood,” Daniel and his friends have many opportunities to take turns at school and while playing at the pool.
sources.supports: Practising in advance how to ask for a turn with words, including asking for a shorter turn; a children's story (Daniel Tiger's Neighborhood) used to model taking turns. A US public media parenting article.

sources.title: Getting Preschoolers to Share…How Do You Do It?
sources.publisher: Pathways.org (pediatric therapists' nonprofit, last updated 18 Jul 2025)
sources.quote: If your child has a toy that is their absolute favorite that they do not want to share, put it away before the play date! ... Something visual, like a timer, will let children know exactly when it’s time for them to give up a certain toy.
sources.supports: A favorite toy can be put away before a playdate; a visual timer shows when it is time to hand over a toy.
